Configure your server

Docker computers

Limit what each local Docker computer can use, keep it off your network, and share host folders with it.

The Docker supervisor is not published as its own image and is not exposed on the host. It runs from the app image, stays on the internal Compose network, and holds the Docker socket because access to it is equivalent to control of the Docker host. Docker sandboxes require SANDBOX_SUPERVISOR_TOKEN (API, worker, supervisor). SCREEN_PROXY_SECRET signs browser-screen capabilities (API and web proxy). Keep both distinct from BETTER_AUTH_SECRET.

Resource ceilings

Each Docker computer runs Xvfb, a window manager and a full Chromium driven by an agent that decides for itself what to open, so it is capped. These defaults provide a starting point for the Docker computer topology:

Variable Default Accepts
RAKAZO_COMPUTER_MEMORY 2g 2g, 1536m, a byte count. Minimum 6m, Docker’s own floor. Also caps swap, so the ceiling holds.
RAKAZO_COMPUTER_CPUS 2 Whole or fractional cores, e.g. 1.5
RAKAZO_COMPUTER_PIDS_LIMIT 2048 A positive integer

Set any of them to 0, none or unlimited to remove that ceiling. A malformed value fails the supervisor at startup naming the variable, rather than surfacing later as a failed bot.

Two caps bound how many computers exist. SANDBOX_MAX_COMPUTERS_PER_USER caps the computers one user’s bots may have, and SANDBOX_MAX_COMPUTERS_PER_SPACE caps concurrent computer containers per Space. SANDBOX_TEAM_SCREEN_LIMIT caps active bot desktops on one Team Computer; desktops and browsers otherwise start only when needed. 0, the default, leaves each to the machine.

The supervisor reaches Docker at /var/run/docker.sock (or //./pipe/docker_engine on Windows). Set DOCKER_SOCKET for rootless Docker, Colima or another path; DOCKER_HOST wins when both are set.

Restricted computer egress

Restricted egress gives Docker computers the public internet (browsing, DNS, apt, git over SSH) but not the Docker host, the LAN, or link-local cloud metadata such as 169.254.169.254, which on a cloud VM would hand instance credentials to anything a bot runs.

It takes two parts:

  1. SANDBOX_COMPUTER_EGRESS=restricted gives each computer network a deterministic host bridge name (rakazo-c…) instead of a generic br-*.

  2. The host ruleset, applied once per Docker host:

    sudo bash infra/compose/restrict-computer-egress.sh

    install-images.sh downloads and runs it (asking for sudo) and records the result in .env. Where the rules cannot be installed (macOS, Windows, Docker Desktop, rootless Docker, no iptables, or a failed run) it writes SANDBOX_COMPUTER_EGRESS=open and says why. The script drops forwarded traffic from rakazo-c* bridges to all non-public IPv4/IPv6 destinations via the DOCKER-USER chain, adds an INPUT drop so computers cannot open connections to the host (established replies to host-initiated control and screen connections still flow), and installs a systemd oneshot so the rules return after a reboot. --print shows the exact rules without changing anything; --remove uninstalls.

Before the first restricted computer starts, the supervisor checks that the host drops connections from a rakazo-c* bridge. Without the ruleset, computers fail to start with an error naming the script instead of running unrestricted; run the script (no restart needed) or set SANDBOX_COMPUTER_EGRESS=open and recreate the supervisor.

When SANDBOX_COMPUTER_EGRESS is unset, the Compose files use auto: the supervisor runs the same check and uses restricted egress if the ruleset is in place, otherwise open egress with a warning in its log. It keeps the first completed answer; a check that could not finish (a Docker error or timeout) fails that computer’s start and runs again on the next one. With the ruleset in place, so does a configured SANDBOX_COMPUTER_DNS that no server answers (see below). An install from before the ruleset existed therefore keeps working when it upgrades. After installing the ruleset, recreate the supervisor, or set restricted to refuse computers whenever the rules are missing. A host-run supervisor (pnpm dev) and the desktop app’s This computer stack default to open: Docker Desktop keeps its bridges in a VM the host rules cannot reach.

Screen streaming is unaffected: the supervisor and web proxy join each computer’s bridge, and the ruleset exempts traffic whose in- and out-interface are both rakazo-c* before any drop (that exemption is load-bearing on hosts where br_netfilter feeds bridged frames through FORWARD). Rules match interface names rather than subnets, so computer create/delete cycles need no firewall maintenance; deleting a computer removes its traffic from the match and nothing else. A computer provisioned while egress was open is replaced on its next provision — resuming it on an unnamed bridge would bypass the restriction.

Computers resolve names through Docker’s embedded DNS. Docker 28 and newer forward lookups to the host’s own resolvers from the host’s network, so a private host resolver (a cloud VPC resolver, a LAN router) keeps working. Older Docker versions forward from the computer’s network, and so does any server set in SANDBOX_COMPUTER_DNS or the daemon’s dns option; the ruleset drops those lookups when the resolver has a private address, and every lookup times out while connections by IP still work. In those cases set SANDBOX_COMPUTER_DNS to public resolvers (comma-separated IP addresses, such as 1.1.1.1,1.0.0.1) and recreate the supervisor; each computer picks the servers up on its next provision. When SANDBOX_COMPUTER_DNS is set, computers with restricted or auto egress start only after one of its first three servers (Docker uses no more) answers from a computer network; a start that fails this check retries it on the next start. The check runs from an IPv4-only network and skips IPv6 servers, so if those three are all IPv6 nothing is checked.

Opening egress

If computers must reach LAN services, an internal proxy, or endpoints bound to the host, set SANDBOX_COMPUTER_EGRESS=open, recreate the supervisor, and run sudo bash infra/compose/restrict-computer-egress.sh --remove. The flag alone does not uninstall the host rules, which keep matching the still-named rakazo-c* bridges until removed.

The ruleset requires Linux Docker Engine with the iptables backend; Docker Desktop, rootless Docker, and firewall-backend: nftables are unsupported. The SANDBOX_SCREEN_NETWORK=internal topology shares one network instead of per-bot bridges, so the mode does not apply there.

Docker in a Linux VM

Where Docker Engine runs in a Linux VM, as with OrbStack on macOS, the rules belong in the VM, which sudo on the host cannot reach. Apply them from a container on the VM’s host network instead, and keep it running: the VM does not persist the rules, so a loop puts them back after a restart. The installer does not download the script on macOS. From the directory that holds the stack’s .env:

curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elie222/rakazo/main/infra/compose/restrict-computer-egress.sh

Save the following as egress.yml beside that script and start it with docker compose -f egress.yml up -d. The name keeps it in its own Compose project:

name: rakazo-computer-egress
services:
  computer-egress:
    image: alpine:3
    network_mode: host
    cap_add: [NET_ADMIN, NET_RAW]
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./restrict-computer-egress.sh:/restrict-computer-egress.sh:ro
    command: >-
      sh -c "apk add --no-cache bash iptables ip6tables &&
      while true; do bash /restrict-computer-egress.sh --apply; sleep 60; done"

Then change SANDBOX_COMPUTER_EGRESS from open to restricted in .env and recreate the supervisor. Docker Desktop has not been tested this way.

IPv6 for computers

Computer networks are created with IPv6 in open egress mode (Docker Engine 27+): Docker allocates a private ULA /64 per network and masquerades outbound traffic through the host’s IPv6 address, so computers reach IPv6-only sites, while names with both address families stay on IPv4 (RFC 6724 address selection with a ULA source). Restricted egress stays IPv4-only: the host ruleset and the startup check enforce and verify IPv4 only. An existing computer picks IPv6 up when its network is created again: a stop releases the network, and the next start creates a new one. Docker 26, Docker-in-Docker without ip6_tables and hosts with IPv6 disabled fall back to IPv4-only networks; the supervisor logs a warning and computers start unchanged. A computer can also stay on IPv4 for longer when its IPv4-only network could not be removed (another user keeps it); IPv4 keeps working, and IPv6 returns once that network is gone — for example after docker network rm of the computer’s rakazo-computer-* network while it is stopped.

Shared host folders

SANDBOX_COMPUTER_MOUNTS mounts host directories into every bot computer (Docker sandboxes only): comma-separated source:target[:option...] entries, for example /srv/team-docs:/mnt/team-docs. Mounts are read-only unless the entry adds rw; rslave is the other option and requires rw, because mounts that reach the computer later keep their own write access. Both paths must be absolute without .., and targets must sit below /mnt, /media or /srv. On Docker Desktop for Windows, write a source in its WSL form (/mnt/c/Users/me/Docs for C:\Users\me\Docs); Docker rejects the Windows form, and rslave does not work on these folders.

The setting is deployment-wide: every bot in every Space sees every mount, and with rw any of them can change or delete what another Space’s bots read. Mount only what all of them may see. The supervisor rejects a source that is, holds, or sits inside the Docker socket, /run, /var/run, /proc, /sys, /dev, /etc, /boot, /root, /var/lib/docker or the data directory that holds bot homes. It compares the configured path, and Docker follows host symlinks, so never point a source at one of these through a symlink.

When the source holds a mount that can be replaced while computers run, such as an SSHFS or NFS share that reconnects, mount the share one level below the source (/srv/shares/docs, with source /srv/shares) and add rw:rslave, so the new mount reaches running computers instead of leaving them on the dead one. Mounting the share at the source itself does not work: replacing it leaves running computers on the old one.

rslave also needs the source to sit on a shared or slave host mount. Check with findmnt -no PROPAGATION -T <source>; systemd hosts report shared for most paths. If it reports private, Docker refuses to create the computer, so make the source its own shared mount first (sudo mount --rbind <source> <source> then sudo mount --make-rshared <source>; --rbind keeps a share already mounted below the source visible. Repeat it at boot, before the share mounts, for example from a systemd mount unit the share’s unit depends on). The source must exist on the Docker host. Recreate the supervisor after a change; each computer picks the new set up on its next provision, which replaces it.

Time zone and language

Each computer runs in its owner’s time zone and app language when the account has them: the supervisor sets TZ and LANGUAGE on the container, and the browser offers pages that language (Accept-Language and navigator.languages), also for a browser profile saved earlier. Without them, the computer stays on UTC and the browser’s default language. A changed time zone or language replaces the computer on its next start, so after upgrading, each computer whose owner has either set is replaced once. The home and saved browser profiles are kept. A custom computer image should not set TZ or LANGUAGE: the computer gets them from the account.
